"Across, down, corner to corner — all the same."

story.zh:
**二试 · 脑子。**

一试下来，站在石阶顶上的，不过四五百人。

二试是在山门里头的一片石坪上考的。石坪上立着几十面石壁，每面石壁上刻着九个空格，横三竖三，像一张棋盘；石壁底下堆着九块石头，每块刻一个数，从一到九。一个管二试的老执事，背着手在石壁前走来走去，道：「横着加，竖着加，斜着加，都要一样。一炷香。」

有人把石头摆成了一朵花，有人摞成了一座塔，有人两块两块地换来换去，换了半炷香，越换越乱，把自己换哭了。还有一个孩子，盯着那九块石头看了很久很久，然后把它们一块一块，全都塞进了嘴里。老执事走过去，叹了口气，在那孩子背上一拍，「噗噗噗」，九块石头吐了一地。老执事对旁边的执事道：「每三年都有一个。」旁边那执事道：「今年这个塞得多，上一回那个只塞了五块。」老执事点点头，道：「一届比一届饿。」

石坪外头有一道矮墙，墙头上探着两颗脑袋，一颗是马家的家丁，一颗是葛六。葛六伸出指头来比划：先四根，再九根，再两根，一排一排地比，比得又快又稳，像镖局里对暗号。马小宝蹲在石壁底下，一面嚼桂花糕，一面照着比划摆石头。香才烧下去一小截，他已经拍拍手站了起来。横着加，十五；竖着加，十五；斜着加，还是十五。他摆完了，特地踱到小满跟前，伸着脖子看了一眼，道：「哟，沈小满，还没摆好？你娘没教你？」

他娘是教过的。那是一句口诀，他娘说，是她爹从一本旧书上看来的：「戴九履一，左三右七，二四为肩，六八为足，五居中央。」小满照着摆：五搁在正当中；头顶戴九，脚下踩一；左手三，右手七。摆到两个肩膀，他的手停住了。二和四，哪一个在左肩，哪一个在右肩？口诀没有说。他把二搁在左肩，四搁在右肩，往下一加：左边这一竖，二加三，再加脚底下那一块，要凑十五，得是一个十。九块石头里，没有十。

铜炉里那炷香，已经烧过了一半。马小宝站在旁边，嚼桂花糕嚼得「吧唧吧唧」响。小满把手从石头上拿开了。他想：口诀记不全，就别背了，算。他娘教他算账，头一句便是：先算总数。

一到九，九块石头，加起来是四十五。横着三排，排排一样多，四十五分成三份，一排是十五。竖着、斜着，也都得是十五。这是总账。再看正当中那一格：横的一条、竖的一条、斜的两条，四条线都从它身上过。每条线上，除了它，还剩两头，两头加起来，得是十五减去它。九块石头要两两配成一样多的对子，只有一种配法：一配九，二配八，三配七，四配六，每对都是十——剩下没配上的那一块，是五。所以五居中央，那四对，隔着五，两两相望。
story.en:
**Second trial · Head.**

After the first trial, those standing at the top of the stair were no more than four or five hundred.

The second trial was held on a stone terrace inside the gate. Dozens of stone walls stood on it, each carved with nine empty squares, three across and three down, like a game board; under each lay nine stones, each carved with a number from one to nine. The old steward in charge of the second trial paced before the walls, hands behind his back. "Add across, add down, add corner to corner — all the same. One stick of incense."

Some arranged the stones into a flower, some stacked them into a pagoda, some swapped them two by two back and forth for half a stick of incense, the more they swapped the worse it got, till they swapped themselves into tears. One boy stared at the nine stones a long, long time, and then put them one by one into his mouth, all nine. The old steward went over, sighed, and slapped him on the back — *pu, pu, pu* — nine stones spat out on the ground. The old steward said to the steward beside him: "Every three years there's one." The other said: "This year's stuffed in more. Last time's only managed five." The old steward nodded. "Hungrier every intake."

Outside the terrace ran a low wall, and over the top of it peeked two heads: one a Ma servant, the other Ge Liu. Ge Liu was signing with his fingers: four, then nine, then two, row by row, fast and steady, like passwords at the escort bureau. Ma Xiaobao squatted at the foot of his wall, chewing osmanthus cake, setting stones by the signs. The incense had burned down only a little when he dusted off his hands and stood. Across, fifteen; down, fifteen; corner to corner, fifteen too. Finished, he strolled over to Xiaoman on purpose and craned his neck. "Well, Shen Xiaoman, not done yet? Didn't your mum teach you?"

His mother had. It was a rhyme; she said her father had got it from an old book: "Wear nine, tread one; three on the left, seven on the right; two and four for shoulders, six and eight for feet; five in the middle." Xiaoman set the stones by it: five in the very middle; nine worn on the head, one trodden under foot; three at the left hand, seven at the right. At the shoulders his hand stopped. Two and four — which on the left shoulder, which on the right? The rhyme didn't say. He put two on the left shoulder and four on the right and added down: the left column, two plus three, plus the stone at the foot — to make fifteen it would have to be ten. Among nine stones there was no ten.

The incense in the burner had burned past half. Ma Xiaobao stood beside him, chomping osmanthus cake with loud smacks. Xiaoman took his hand off the stones. He thought: if I can't remember the rhyme whole, stop reciting — reckon. When his mother taught him accounts, the very first line was: first reckon the total.

One to nine, nine stones, add up to forty-five. Three rows across, each the same, forty-five split three ways: fifteen a row. Down and corner to corner, fifteen too. That was the total. Now the middle square: one line across, one down, two corner to corner — four lines all pass through it. On each line, besides it, there are two ends, and the two ends must add up to fifteen less the middle. For nine stones to pair off into equal pairs there's only one way: one with nine, two with eight, three with seven, four with six, each pair ten — and the one stone left unpaired is five. So five sits in the middle, and the four pairs face each other across it.

exits.means: hands in the solved square, or asks to go on to the third trial

refuse.zh: 九宫还没填满。瞿老不看半张卷子。
refuse.en: The square is not filled yet. Elder Qu does not look at half an answer.

story.zh:
有了这个，肩膀就好办了。头顶是九，九的两边加起来得是六；剩下的石头里，凑得出六的，只有二和四。左手是三，左肩和左脚加起来得是十二；二和四里头，配得出十二的只有四——四配八。所以左肩是四，左脚是八；右肩是二，右脚是六。口诀一个字也没错，它只是没说，哪边是左。小满一块一块摆好了：横着加，十五；竖着加，十五；斜着加，十五。炉里的香，还剩一小截。

老执事先踱到马小宝那面石壁前，看了一会儿，点点头，问道：「五为什么在中间？」马小宝一愣，眼睛往墙头上溜。墙头上，葛六急得伸出五根手指头，又拍了拍自己的肚子——意思是「五，正当中」。马小宝看明白了，大声道：「因为肚子在中间！」

石坪上登时笑成了一片。老执事顺着马小宝的眼睛往墙头上一看，看见了葛六，眉毛一挑：「葛六？」墙头上那颗脑袋「嗖」地缩了回去。老执事道：「二十年前，你那个『五』，也是背的。」他在马小宝的考牌上画了一笔——画的不是一道，是一个圈。马小宝的脸白了。绳子外头，马三隔着衣裳，又按了一按怀里那封信。

老执事又踱到小满跟前，问的还是那一句：「五为什么在中间？」小满便把一对一对的配法说了一遍。老执事听完，半天没说话，末了道：「谁教你的？」小满道：「口诀是我娘教的。为什么，是我方才算的。」

老执事「嗯」了一声，在他考牌上画了一道，却没有走，在石壁跟前一块石头上坐了下来，捶着腰道：「这叫洛书。《周易·系辞上》里有一句：『河出图，洛出书，圣人则之。』后人说，禹治水的时候得了它，照着这九个格子，把天下分成了九州，又收了九州的铜，铸了九口鼎，一州一口。」说到这里，他顿了一顿，朝身后那座山看了一眼，声音低了些，「——这都是老辈子的话了。你娘教得好。你算得也好。」

小满把「九口鼎」三个字在嘴里嚼了一遍。九口大锅，一州一口，那得煮多少饭。他觉得胸口那块木牌好像动了一下，伸手去摸，却是凉的。

他转过身，石坪那一头，另一面石壁前，早有人摆好了。一个红鼻头的姑娘，蹲在石壁底下，拿一根炭条，在一个巴掌大的小本子上，低着头记着什么。小满不由得一愣：这年头，谁出门考仙门，还随身带个本子记账？他往那边挤了两步，人群一涌，再抬头看时，那石壁底下已经空了，只地上留着一截用秃了的炭条头。
story.en:
With that, the shoulders were easy. Nine on the head, so the two beside it must make six; of the stones left, only two and four make six. Three at the left hand, so the left shoulder and left foot must make twelve; of two and four, only four can pair to twelve — four with eight. So the left shoulder is four and the left foot eight; the right shoulder two, the right foot six. The rhyme hadn't got a word wrong; it just never said which side was left. Xiaoman set them one by one: across, fifteen; down, fifteen; corner to corner, fifteen. A little stub of incense was left.

The old steward went first to Ma Xiaobao's wall, looked a while, nodded, and asked: "Why is five in the middle?" Ma Xiaobao froze, his eyes sliding to the top of the wall. On the wall, Ge Liu, frantic, held up five fingers and patted his own belly — meaning: "five, right in the middle". Ma Xiaobao got it and said loudly: "Because the belly's in the middle!"

The whole terrace burst out laughing. The old steward followed Ma Xiaobao's eyes up to the wall, saw Ge Liu, and raised an eyebrow. "Ge Liu?" The head on the wall shot down out of sight. The old steward said: "Twenty years ago, that 'five' of yours was learned by rote too." He drew a mark on Ma Xiaobao's tag — not a stroke: a circle. Ma Xiaobao's face went white. Outside the rope Ma San pressed the letter in his coat again, through the cloth.

The old steward strolled over to Xiaoman and asked the same: "Why is five in the middle?" Xiaoman told him the pairing, pair by pair. The old steward heard him out and said nothing for a long while; at last: "Who taught you?" Xiaoman said: "The rhyme my mother taught me. The why, I just reckoned."

The old steward grunted, drew a stroke on his tag, but didn't leave; he sat down on a stone by the wall, thumped his back, and said: "This is called the Luo Shu. The *Book of Changes*, in the Great Commentary, has a line: 'The Yellow River brought forth the Chart, the Luo brought forth the Writing, and the sages took them as their pattern.' Later people said Yu got it while taming the flood, and by these nine squares divided the world into nine provinces, and gathered the bronze of the nine provinces and cast nine *ding*, one for each province." Here he paused, glanced at the mountain behind him, and lowered his voice. "— All old people's talk. Your mother taught you well. And you reckoned well."

Xiaoman chewed the words "nine *ding*" over once. Nine big pots, one a province — that would cook a lot of rice. He felt the token on his chest seem to stir; he reached for it, and it was cool.

He turned round. At the far end of the terrace, before another wall, someone had long since finished — a girl with a red nose, squatting at the foot of the wall, a stick of charcoal in hand, head down, writing something in a palm-sized notebook. Xiaoman stared: these days, who comes to sit the immortal trials carrying a notebook to keep accounts? He pushed two steps that way; the crowd surged, and when he looked up again the foot of the wall was empty, only a worn-down stub of charcoal left on the ground.
